title: Taylor's Chocolate Chip Cookie Recipe
contents:
Ingredients
1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter
3/4 cup granulated sugar
3/4 cup brown sugar
1 tsp vanilla extract
2 eggs
2 1/4 cups all purpose flour
1 tsp salt
1 tsp baking soda
2 cups your chocolate of choice (chips or small pieces)
Flaky salt for sprinkling
Step 1: Brown the butter
In a small saucepan, melt and cook the butter until the sputtering subsides, and the floating bits of solids start to turn brown. The butter will smell fragrant and nutty. Once it reaches this stage, immediately transfer to a heat proof bowl (make sure to scrape the brown bits off the bottom) and place in the freezer to solidify. We want this butter to be soft, not melted but not frozen solid. Check on it every few mins.
Step 2: Mix wet ingredients
Once butter is somewhat more solid, transfer to a mixing bowl, and add both sugars. Beat together until creamy and fluffy.
Add eggs and vanilla, and beat until smooth.
Step 3: Add dry ingredients
Add flour, baking soda and salt, and mix until the dough comes together.
Step 4: Add chocolate
Gently fold in your chocolate of choice. My personal favorite is Trader Joe’s Pound Plus Milk Chocolate Bar with Caramel, Pretzel, Sea Salt. But of course it’s seasonal and only available in winter.
Step 5: Portion & chill
Portion your dough out onto a lined baking tray. I like to use a cookie scoop for even sizes. You can overcrowd your pan since we are not baking yet.
Place portioned dough in the fridge for at least 1 hour. This is important for texture!!
Step 6: Salt & bake
Preheat oven to 375F
Place a couple dough balls onto a new lined baking sheet. Make sure to space out evenly.
Top with a sprinkle of Maldon flaky salt on each cookie
Bake in oven for 10-15 mins, or until starting to turn golden brown
Try not to eat them all at once!

title: 2025 Reading Challenge
description: A yearlong reading quest shaped by friendship, curiosity, and unexpected bookish adventures. (Beware - spice ahead)
contents:
Contents
Introduction
The Challenges

Introduction
For the past few years I’ve challenged myself to read one more book per year than the last. It’s been great motivation, but I’ve found myself getting a bit bored in my reading patterns. So this year I’ve designed a new challenge: one book per month - 12 books total - each with a different theme chosen by a friend or family member.
As I solicited themes and genres from my loved ones, I was surprised at just how creative people got with the themes - and how many people wanted to join me in my quest!
The Challenges
📚 2025 Monthly Reading Challenge

🌟 Bonus Books
Lady Tan’s Circle of Women (Kat)
A book written by Shelby Cleland
Go to your last 5-star read on Goodreads, then go to that author’s page, and read another one of their 5-star rated reads. (Shelby)
A book with recipes in it that is not a cookbook (Haley)
Specific recommendation: Mad Honey

Monthly Recaps
January: A short story or essay in your career field or a field you are interested in.

  
    
      
  
  
    Theme suggested by: Kalani
    What I read: Holy Water by Joan Didion
  

Why I picked it: This book was suggested by a friend of mine that used to work in a similar field (water). I also started this theme late in the month, and a short read was just what I needed.
My thoughts: Didion opens, “Some of us who live in arid parts of the world think about water with a reverence others might find excessive.” This was not the case for my household. I was raised to believe that water simply came from the tap - and never gave any thought to where it came from before it made it to my kitchen sink. So long as the faucet worked, nothing else really mattered. This is in stark contrast to the field I work in now, where I not only give great thought to where a utility’s water comes from, but am constantly working towards accounting for every last drop.
Didion’s essay is a poetic reflection on the physical movement of water through the arid state of California, and how this all-important aspect of life balances on a thin edge of control, dictated by a myriad of agencies: “Los Angeles moves some of it, San Francisco moves some of it, the Bureau of Reclamation’s Central Valley Project moves some of it, and the California State Water Project moves most of the rest of it, moves a vast amount of it, moves more water farther than has ever been moved anywhere.”
But what really struck me in this essay was a singular line: “The apparent ease of California life is an illusion, and those who believe the illusion real live here in only the most temporary way.” I’ve re-read this line a hundred times, and it captures the essence of Southern California in such a stark, raw way. Life in California is by no means easy, and those who do believe it to be so are those who only pass through - they don’t stay.
While I may have not understood the significance of the water making its way to my tap as a child, I did have an inkling that not many people who came to California stay. The Los Angeles elite I saw on TV had no idea a little girl from the desert a hundred miles away watched them, and after their red carpet event, they’d jet away to the next location with no thought to the complex network of waterworks that made their event possible, just as I gave no thought to the water in my kitchen tap.
February: A book with a color, plant, or food in it’s name.

  
    
  
    Theme suggested by: Kat
    What I read: Braiding Sweetgrass by Robin Wall Kimmerer
  

Why I picked it: This book had been a work in progress for me for almost a year. I figured this month’s theme was the perfect motivation I needed to actually finish it.
My thoughts: This book was beautifully written, but I also have realized that I struggle to read long form non-fiction. I had started the book in 2024, and had fallen asleep nearly every time I read it.
It was once I realized that I needed to take each chapter as a sort of short-form essay that I began to make progress. Each chapter is in itself a beautiful piece of writing, but when woven together with the other chapters in its section, make a cohesive whole, just as the sweetgrass stalks are woven together in Kimmerer’s stories.
I am left after reading this book with a feeling of great respect for this work, but the feeling that I missed much of the message. I think I’ll have to slowly re-read this book with my piecemeal methodology to further digest the meaning and calls to action.
March: Smut - or romance if that’s more your vibe.

  
    
  
    Theme suggested by: Frankie
    What I read: The Kiss Quotient by Helen Hoang
  

Why I picked it: I received this book as the result of a spicy book exchange for Galentine’s day.
My thoughts: Loved this. It is definitely not PG, but the spicy scenes were slow-burning and, for lack of a better term, kinda wholesome? (Gotta love consent!)
April: A book that altered someone’s brain chemistry.

  
    
  
    Theme suggested by: Haley
    What I read: By Any Other Name by Jodi Picoult
  

Why I picked it: I LOVE me some Shakespeare and a great historical conspiracy theory. I am also a fan of female-centered stories, so the description of this one was right up my alley.
My thoughts: This book crushed me in so many ways. It was gritty, funny, thought-provoking, beautiful, and heartbreaking all in one. I absolutely loved learning about Emilia Bassano and her real-life connections to potential authorship of some of The Bard’s greatest works.
As much as I loved the story and speculation of this book, I found it to be the next book in a line that has disappointed me with its graphic use of violence to showcase a woman’s growth of character. While I understand much of Emilia’s story is based on the fact that she was a courtesan, she was hardly a willing one - and underage at that. To say nothing of her abusive husband later in life. I am extremely tired of a woman finding and defining her worth “in spite of all her hardships.” For once I would like those hardships to not be sexual or physical violence. A woman is so much more than the level of violence she endures.
Which segues nicely into a broader discussion at the heart of this book: If a woman can be defined by what she does rather than what happens to her, how important is it for that woman to receive the proper credit for her works? In other words, of what significance is it to separate the art from the artist? In Emilia’s case, she sacrificed her own credit so that her art could see the light of day. But that same art carries a different weight and meaning with a different name on it. I don’t think this is a question that can be answered in a blog post, but it gave me so much to think about for weeks after I finished it. I highly recommend this book with a strong trigger warning caveat.
May: A middle grade book

  
    
  
    Theme suggested by: Shelby
    What I read: Island of the Blue Dolphins by Scott O'Dell
  

Why I picked it:
My thoughts:
June: A book by a trans or non-binary author

  
    
  
    Theme suggested by: Alana
    What I read: Confessions of the Fox by Jordy Rosenberg
  

Why I picked it: I tend to have a hard time reading contemporary stories, so the rough-and-tumble underbelly of 1700s England piqued my interest with this historical fantasy.
My thoughts: Like By Any Other Name, Confessions of the Fox made me think in ways I never had before. I had never read a story that was essentially two stories, one inside the other. The story of Jack Shepphard is told by Dr. R. Voth, who concurrently tells his own story by way of footnotes throughout his processing of mysterious manuscript that claims to tell Shepphard’s true story.
One theme I found especially intriguing was the idea that Jack’s story was not merely his own, but a collective history written by and for trans and queer people. Jack’s story stands as a sort of folk hero-esque vehicle for which those marginalized groups share their own experiences, views of the world, and histories. So while the “true” story of the “real” Jack may not be faithfully told, a wider, more nuanced and varied picture is revealed.
July: A book that made someone cry

title: Earth Month 2025
description: Join me as I harass my friends with fun facts and calls to action for Earth Month 2025.
contents:
Background
As an environmental scientist and all-around nerd, it is my moral duty to inform the people I love about all things Earth, ecology, policy, and anything else that affects our natural world. As such, April is my favorite month of the year, and Earth Day my patron holiday.
A few years ago I started texting fun facts to my various friends’ group chats following the theme of Earth Month. It became very well-received (or maybe they’re just nice to me idk), so this year I decided to write it all down here for your enjoyment as well.
So please join me in annoying my friends with various Earth Month fun facts, calls to action, rage and hope all at once.
Welcome
🚨 ATTENTION 🚨
You have all been involuntarily enrolled in Taylor’s Earth Month Facts™️, a weekly dose of eco-truths, because knowledge is power and ignorance is trash (and we do NOT litter). Unsubscribe? Not an option. Stay tuned, tree huggers. 🌎💅
Week 1: The Comeback of the Channel Islands Fox
Wayyyyyy back when (aka in the ’90s) the Channel Islands fox was circling the extinction drain—fewer than 100 left. The culprits? An ecological chain reaction of the worst kind. DDT wiped out bald eagles, which let golden eagles move in, who then started hunting foxes (instead of their usual fishy snacks). Add in some non-native pigs attracting even more golden eagles, and things got bad fast.
But humans (for once) stepped up with an ambitious recovery plan: Pigs? Removed. Golden eagles? Relocated. Bald eagles? Reintroduced. Foxes? Given a serious population boost.
Thanks to these efforts, the Channel Islands Fox made the fastest recovery of any endangered mammal in U.S. history. By 2016, it was officially removed from the Endangered Species List.
Moral of the story? Ecosystems are like Jenga—pull out the wrong piece (or, you know, poison everything with DDT), and the whole thing collapses. But a little human help (when done right) can make all the difference. We can fix what is broken. 🦊 🦅 🐟
Bonus Earth Month Fact: Our parks need us.
It’s National Park Advocacy Week, and our national parks are hurting—crumbling trails, understaffed crews, and climate threats stacking up.
Despite all the love parks get, the current administration has proposed major fuckery funding and staffing cuts that would make things worse.
Groups like NPCA are pushing back—demanding Congress fund, fix, and fight for our parks.
Quick action: Use this page to tell your reps to take care of the places we all love:
Prevent Further Cuts to Park Staff and Funding
Week 2: The War for Water in the West
Happy Earth Month, babes — today’s tea: a good old-fashioned government turf war 🫖. The Bureau of Reclamation and the Army Corps of Engineers went head-to-head over who got to control the West’s water. Spoiler: it was messy.
In the early 1900s, two government agencies were basically in a turf war over who got to play water god in the American West.
💧 The Bureau of Reclamation was created in 1902 to build dams and irrigation projects for small farmers. Their goal? Turn the arid West into an agricultural paradise.
⚓️ The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers focused on big river navigation and flood control, mainly in the East and South. But they weren’t about to let Reclamation have all the fun.
For decades, these two fought over who controlled dam-building, water rights, and which projects got funded. The rivalry peaked in the 1930s with massive projects like Hoover Dam (Reclamation’s crown jewel) and Bonneville Dam (the Corps’ big win on the Columbia River).
Today, both agencies still shape U.S. water policy—Reclamation dominates the West, while the Army Corps rules the East. But the legacy of their “dam rivalry” lives on in America’s sprawling network of reservoirs, irrigation canals, and hydroelectric power. 🚰
Week 3: How the US Almost Ran Out of Birds
Aloha nerds. Here’s your Earth Month Fun Fact:
In the late 1800s and early 1900s, the U.S. came dangerously close to running out of birds — thanks to fashion. Wealthy women were flaunting hats covered in entire birds, not just feathers. We’re talking herons, egrets, owls, even hummingbirds. At the height of the feather craze, some rookeries were being wiped out entirely in a single nesting season just to meet demand.
Hunters were paid to collect feathers—and they did it by the pound. Egrets were especially prized for their delicate plumes, which, fun fact, they only grow during breeding season… meaning the birds were often killed right on their nests, leaving chicks to die. Cute look, huh?
By the early 20th century, bird populations had crashed, and a lot of Americans were like, “Oops?” But not everyone. A group of fierce, fed-up women started organizing—boycotting feathered hats, forming Audubon Societies, and lobbying for laws to stop the slaughter. Their activism helped lead to the Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918, which still protects birds today.
So yes, we almost ran out of birds. But thanks to a few bold women who refused to let fashion kill off entire species, we didn’t. Feathers are for birds, not bonnets. 🪶🪿🦆
Bonus Earth Month Content: Ologies Podcast
My fave podcast has an episode on garbage and sanitation that I highly recommend. Not something you think about often, but so incredibly important to a functioning society.
Ologies: Discard Anthropology (GARBAGE) Encore with Robin Nagle
Week 4: Earth Day
Happy Earth Day nerds 🌎
In honor of the holiday you get this week’s Earth Month fact a day early. Apologies if you’ve heard this one before but I love it so much and it hits close to home.
Earth Day Exists Because One Guy Got Mad About an Oil Spill—and a Bunch of Hippies, Housewives, and Students Showed Up
In 1969, a massive oil spill off the coast of Santa Barbara turned beaches into sludge and killed thousands of seabirds. It was disgusting, it was devastating, and it was the last straw for Senator Gaylord Nelson (side note: best name ever). He had an idea: what if Americans came together just one day a year to demand a cleaner planet?
So in 1970, the first Earth Day was born. No big budget, no social media—just 20 million people (10% of the U.S. population at the time!) marching, striking, and calling for action. The crowd was a glorious mess of students, farmers, teachers, housewives, and Vietnam War protestors who all agreed on one thing: the Earth was in trouble, and it was time to do something.
And it worked. That first Earth Day helped lead to the creation of the EPA, the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act, and more. (Which are all currently in danger but that’s a story for another time)
So next time my parents someone rolls their eyes at your reusable water bottle, remind them that one angry senator and a whole lot of everyday people helped change the course of environmental history.
Happy Earth Day. The planet is lucky to have you. 💙💚
